metadata.description: Two near-contemporaneous (2012) RLWE-based FHE constructions that share the same foundations (RLWE hardness, ring expansion factor, B-bounded noise, the LPR public-key scheme, and a noise-controlled multiplication-then-relinearisation/refresh pipeline) but differ in plaintext encoding: BGV places the message in the least-significant bits and uses a ladder of moduli with modulus-switching at every level to manage noise, whereas BFV scales the message by Delta = floor(q/t) and absorbs noise growth into a single large modulus. Their relinearisation/key-switching primitives correspond directly (digit-decomposition <-> BitDecomp/Powersof2, modulus-switching relin <-> Scale + SwitchKey). Parallel rediscovery / parallel formulation of the same underlying scheme.

matches.explanation: Both define a B-bounded distribution as one whose samples lie in [-B,B] (BFV) or exceed B with negligible probability (BGV). Standard noise-distribution definition used identically by both schemes to bound the magnitude of fresh-encryption noise.

Both define the decision Ring-LWE problem over the cyclotomic ring R = Z[x]/(x^d+1) (or general cyclotomic in BFV): distinguish (a, a*s + e) samples from uniform on R_q^2. Same external citation (Lyubashevsky-Peikert-Regev 2010); same hardness assumption underpinning each scheme.

Both define the ring expansion factor (gamma_R in BGV, delta_R in BFV) as the worst-case multiplicative blow-up of norm under ring multiplication, which appears identically in noise-growth bounds for homomorphic multiplication. BFV uses the coefficient sup-norm, BGV uses a Euclidean-style norm; the role in subsequent analysis is the same.

BGV's hardness assumption is GLWE (which subsumes both LWE and RLWE); BFV's hardness assumption is the decision-RLWE problem itself. Specialising GLWE to the n=1 setting recovers RLWE, giving the same security foundation for both schemes; flagged as analogous because the BGV statement is strictly more general and is bundled as an explicit assumption node, whereas BFV folds it into the RLWE definition.

Both invoke a (weak) circular-security assumption. BGV uses circular security to collapse the per-level key ladder to a single key (turning leveled FHE into pure FHE), whereas BFV uses weak circular security to justify publishing the relinearisation key rlk that contains masked T^i*s^2 terms. Same flavour of assumption serving structurally different roles.

Both are the Lyubashevsky-Peikert-Regev (RLWE) public-key encryption scheme. BGV presents it in the GLWE generalisation (LWE/RLWE selector bit); BFV presents the standard cyclotomic-RLWE form with explicit Delta = floor(q/t) scaling. Same SetUp / KeyGen / Enc / Dec template, same security reduction. The Delta scaling vs LSB encoding is the key point of divergence between the two schemes (handled in the next-level matches), but at the base-LPR-encryption layer the algorithms coincide.

Both bound the noise of a fresh ciphertext under the LPR encryption scheme. BGV's LP305.5 gives ||noise|| <= 1 + 2*gamma_R*sqrt(d)*N*B_chi for parameters N = (2 n_L+1) log q_L; BFV's LP306.1 gives ||v|| <= 2 delta_R B^2 + B for the LPR ciphertext, with PP306.1 supplying the (one-line) proof by direct expansion modulo q. Same lemma type (noise bound for fresh encryption) with analogous structure (linear in B_chi, quadratic when including the secret); differences come from BFV's Delta scaling and small-secret assumption.

BGV's Lemma on Add correctness (noise at most doubles) corresponds to BFV's FV.SH.Add algorithm and the additive part of LP306.3 (||v_add|| < 2E + t). Both establish that homomorphic addition is component-wise and roughly doubles the noise; the +t term in BFV reflects the Delta-scaling rounding overhead absent from BGV's LSB encoding.

BGV's pre-Refresh multiplication-noise lemma (||noise|| <= gamma_R B^2) is the BGV analogue of BFV's basic homomorphic multiplication AP306.3 plus its noise bounds LP306.2 and LP306.3 (multiplicative noise ~ E*t*delta_R*(delta_R+1.25)). Both quantify the noise produced by the tensored ciphertext before any noise-management step; BFV's bound includes the t-factor coming from scaled-fractional encoding while BGV's does not.

BGV's SwitchKey/SwitchKeyGen (using BitDecomp+Powersof2 with key tau = A + Powersof2(s_1)) is the same template as BFV's two relinearisation procedures: Version 1 uses base-T digit decomposition (the direct base-2 case is BGV's BitDecomp), and Version 2 uses modulus-switching style relinearisation. BGV's single key-switching primitive plays the role of BFV's two relinearisation variants; supporting lemmas LP305.2 (BitDecomp/Powersof2 identity) and LP305.3 (key-switch correctness) are subsumed in the BFV algorithm specifications.

Cluster correspondence between BGV's bit-decomposition / powers-of-2 relinearisation primitives and BFV's Relin Version 1 (digit-decomposition base T). BGV breaks the construction into separate definitions (BitDecomp, Powersof2), an inner-product identity (LP305.2), correctness (LP305.3) and a noise bound (LP305.9); BFV bundles all of these inside AP306.4 with the implicit base-T identity. Confidence medium because the BFV node is coarser-grained and the identity is implicit there.

Cluster correspondence between BGV's full modulus-switching machinery (Scale primitive DP305.6, integer modulus-switching lemma LP305.1, ring version LP305.4, the noise-reduction corollary CP305.1, and the Switch-Moduli step LP305.8) and BFV's modulus-switching reduction algorithm AP306.9. BGV's lemma chain establishes that rounded scaling by p/q preserves the residue mod 2 and contracts noise by p/q; BFV uses an analogous scaling 2^n/q to map the BFV ciphertext into a power-of-2 modulus for bootstrapping. Same primitive used for fundamentally different purposes (BGV: per-level noise reduction; BFV: pre-bootstrap modulus normalisation).

Both are the main scheme constructions. BGV's FHE Scheme without Bootstrapping is a leveled FHE with a ladder of per-level moduli {q_j} and per-level keys {s_j}, refreshing after each operation; BFV's FV.SH is a single-modulus somewhat-homomorphic scheme that relinearises after each multiplication. Same overall (KeyGen, Enc, Dec, Add, Mul, plus a noise-management routine) interface; differ in encoding (LSB vs scaled Delta) and noise control (modulus ladder vs single modulus + relin).

Composite L2-spanning entry: BGV's FHE.Refresh procedure (with its three algorithm-step children Expand via Powersof2, Switch-Moduli via Scale, Switch-Keys via SwitchKey) corresponds to BFV's two relinearisation algorithms. BFV's Relin Version 1 mirrors the Expand+SwitchKey portion (digit decomposition + key-switched recombination); BFV's Relin Version 2 mirrors the Switch-Moduli portion (working modulo p*q and rescaling). BGV does the three steps every level for noise control; BFV does them once per multiplication for degree reduction. The L2-step DAGs differ in interesting ways (BGV has a strict 3-step linear chain; BFV's two versions are alternatives) so a single composite entry is more informative than per-step matches.

Both are the main correctness-and-depth theorems. BGV's TP305.3 states FHE is correct for L-leveled circuits with per-gate cost O~(d * n_L^3 * L^2); BFV's TP306.1 states FV.SH correctly evaluates depth-L circuits when 4*delta_R^L*(delta_R+1.25)^(L+1)*t^(L-1) < floor(q/B). The flavour is the same (depth bound implied by noise analysis) but the BGV statement is asymptotic and complexity-focused, the BFV statement is explicit-inequality and parameter-focused, reflecting the schemes' different flavours (theoretical leveled-FHE vs concrete-parameters somewhat-FHE).

BGV's encryption equation c = m + A^T r is the LSB-encoding ciphertext form; the analogous BFV ciphertext is encoded inside AP306.1 as (Delta*m + p_0*u + e_1, p_1*u + e_2). Both encrypt by adding masked noise to a (transformed) message; the difference is the message scaling Delta = floor(q/t) in BFV vs LSB-only in BGV.

BGV's multiplication-via-tensoring identity Q_{c_1,c_2}(x) = L_{c_1}(x)*L_{c_2}(x) = L^long_{c_1,c_2}(x tensor x) is the BGV statement of the same algebraic identity that BFV expands explicitly in EP306.1 (full degree-2 product expansion) and EP306.2 (scaled (t/q) approximation). Both papers exploit the fact that the product of two ciphertexts decrypts to the message product under the tensored secret s tensor s (or s, s^2).

BGV's decryption equation m = [[c,s]_q]_2 (LSB extraction) is structurally specific to BGV's LSB encoding. BFV decryption is implicit in AP306.1 / LP306.1 and uses the very different formula round(t/q * [c,s]_q) (Delta-scaled rounding). Marking none rather than analogous because the formulas play the same role but require entirely different decoding (mod 2 vs scaled rounding).

BGV defines noise of a ciphertext explicitly as [c,s]_q with decryption succeeding while it is < q/2. BFV does not introduce a corresponding standalone definition node; the noise is implicit inside Lemma 1 (LP306.1) where v is identified within Delta*m + v. Conceptually the same notion in both papers, but with no isolated definition node on the BFV side to align.

BGV imports Gentry's leveled-FHE definition (parameterised family with shared decryption circuit, depth-L circuit evaluation, complexity polynomial in lambda, L, circuit size). BFV does not introduce a corresponding leveled-FHE definition; it instead works with a single SH scheme plus bootstrapping. External-origin in BGV but the contribution it enables is BGV-specific.

BGV explicitly defines the (vector) LWE problem in addition to RLWE, since GLWE encompasses both. BFV is purely RLWE-based and does not introduce LWE separately. The standalone LWE definition has no BFV counterpart.

GLWE (the unified problem interpolating between LWE at d=1 and RLWE at n=1) is a BGV-specific framing introduced precisely to handle both LWE and RLWE in a single scheme. BFV commits to the RLWE setting from the start and has no GLWE-style generalisation.
BGV defines a ring l_1 norm (sum of coefficient norms) needed for its modulus-switching bounds. BFV uses only the coefficient sup-norm (DP306.2), so this auxiliary norm has no BFV counterpart.

BGV's batched FHE on plaintext slots (Chinese-Remaindering across the d prime ideals to get O~(lambda*L^3 / min(d, ell)) per-gate cost) is a distinctive BGV optimisation. BFV does not develop SIMD/CRT batching in this paper.
BGV's Pack/Unpack algorithms for batched bootstrapping (using ring automorphisms sigma_{1->i}) are BGV-only. BFV has no batching/automorphism layer in this paper.
BGV's lemma optimising the lazy-bootstrapping interval at L = theta(log lambda) is specific to BGV's modulus-ladder cost analysis. BFV does not perform this kind of cost optimisation.
BGV's generalisation of modulus switching to ideal moduli (enabling exponentially large prime plaintext spaces) has no analogue in BFV.

Regev's worst-case-to-average-case LWE reduction is cited explicitly in BGV (external-origin theorem) because BGV uses LWE. BFV cites only RLWE hardness and does not bring in the Regev LWE reduction as a node. External in A but not in B; mark none for completeness.

BGV cites the Lyubashevsky-Peikert-Regev RLWE-to-ideal-SVP reduction as a separate theorem node. BFV references the same hardness foundation only inside the Decision-RLWE definition (DP306.5) and does not introduce a hardness-reduction theorem as a separate node. The underlying cited result is the same; mark none here because the matched RLWE definition already captures the shared assumption.

BGV's public-key relation A*s = 2*e is specific to BGV's LSB-encoding setup: the factor 2 ensures the message bit is preserved under decryption. BFV's analogous public-key relation is built into AP306.1 with no factor-2 structure (BFV uses Delta-scaling instead). No clean BFV counterpart equation.

BGV explicitly states the FHE construction problem as a problem node. BFV motivates the same problem in its introduction but does not introduce a formal problem node; the goal is implicit in AP306.6 (FV.SH) and the bootstrapping construction. No problem-node counterpart in B.

BGV writes out separate proofs for the integer and ring versions of its modulus-switching lemmas (LP305.1, LP305.4): both unwind [c,s]_q = c.s - kq, define e_p = c'.s - kp, and bound ||e_p|| <= (p/q)||[c,s]_q|| + correction. BFV's modulus-switching reduction AP306.9 is presented algorithmically without a separate proof node; the proof content is implicit in AP306.9's noise bound. Marked none rather than analogous because BFV provides no proof-typed counterpart node.

BGV proofs of the BitDecomp/Powersof2 inner-product identity (PP305.2: bilinearity of <BitDecomp(c,q), Powersof2(s,q)>) and key-switching correctness (PP305.3: substitute B*s_2 = 2*e_2 + Powersof2(s_1) and apply Lemma 2). BFV bundles the same algebraic identities inside AP306.4 (Relin V1) without separate proof nodes.

BGV's proof of TP305.3 chooses a universal noise bound B = lambda^a L^b and modulus ladder q_j ~ 2^{(j+1)*omega(log lambda + log L)}, then verifies Property 1 (noise dominates additive errors) and Property 2 (q_j/q_{j-1} >= 2 B gamma_R) and inducts on circuit level. The BFV analogue is the parameter-derivation in TP306.1 / EP306.5, which produces the explicit inequality 4*delta_R^L*(delta_R+1.25)^(L+1)*t^(L-1) < q/B - but is not given a separate proof node. Conceptually corresponds to the TP305.3<->TP306.1 match above.
BGV's proof of LP305.10 (lazy-bootstrapping interval) is BGV-specific; LP305.10 itself has no BFV counterpart, so its proof inherits the same orphan status.

BFV introduces an explicit definition node for the polynomial quotient ring R = Z[x]/(f(x)) and its mod-q reduction R_q. BGV uses the same ring throughout (introduced inline in DP305.4 RLWE and DP305.5 GLWE) but does not factor it into a separate definition node. Conceptually the same setting; flagged none for lack of a matching definition-typed node.

BFV defines the discrete Gaussian D_{Z,sigma} as a concrete instantiation of its noise distribution chi. BGV works abstractly with a B-bounded chi (DP305.3) without committing to a Gaussian; no Gaussian definition node in BGV.

BFV's small-secret optimisation (sample s, u from R_2 with binary coefficients) is a BFV-specific practicality optimisation. BGV does not use binary secrets and has no analogous small-secret assumption.

BFV's H(f) helper quantity (max norm of sum of |x^{i+j} mod f(x)|; equals 1 for f = x^d+1) is used inside its bootstrapping-depth bounds TP306.2/TP306.3. BGV neither bootstraps nor uses this quantity.

BFV's bootstrapping-depth theorem (optimised case q = 2^n, t | q) characterises when FV.SH bootstraps to FV.FH. BGV's whole point is to avoid bootstrapping (its title is 'Fully Homomorphic Encryption without Bootstrapping'); accordingly there is no BGV node corresponding to a bootstrapping-depth theorem. This is the most prominent contrast between the two papers.
BFV's general-case bootstrapping-depth theorem (arbitrary q, t) again has no BGV counterpart for the same reason as TP306.2: BGV avoids bootstrapping by construction.

BFV's BootKeyGen (encrypting each bit of the secret s under pk) is a standard bootstrapping primitive (a la Gentry). BGV explicitly engineers around bootstrapping with its modulus ladder, so it has no BootKeyGen node.

BFV's Bootstrap algorithm (homomorphic decryption circuit using carry-save adders to sum the rounding bit matrix mod 2^S_R) has no BGV counterpart; BGV's noise management is via the modulus ladder + Refresh, never via homomorphic decryption.

BFV's FHE parameter inequality (4*beta(eps)*delta_R^L_max*(delta_R+1.25)^(L_max+1)*t^(L_max-1) < q/sigma) is BFV's parameter-selection inequality combining the depth bound (TP306.1) with the Lindner-Peikert distinguishing condition for security. BGV does not derive an analogous concrete-parameters inequality; its analysis is asymptotic via TP305.3.
